newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan activists storm quasi-Japanese embassy.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan activists storm quasi-Japanese embassy.

text.p: Taiwan activists on Wednesday stormed into the quasi-official embassy of Japan in Taipei to protest at what they called the illegal landing by four Japanese on disputed islands in the East China Sea.
Some 18 activists disguised as visa applicants entered the visa office of Japan's Interchange Association to protest against Tuesday's landing on the islands by a group led by a Japanese legislator.
The association represents Japanese interests in Taiwan in the absence of diplomatic relations.
Shouting "Down with Japanese militarism", the activists from the Taiwan Diaoyu Islands Defence Action Committee pelted office counters and walls with eggs, forcing staff to take cover.
The islands are know as the Diaoyus to the China and the Senkakus to the Japanese.

"Japan is too coercive and shameless. It has repeatedly invaded Chinese territory and now it occupies the Diaoyu islands. Its legislator even landed on the island," said Ching Chia-shou, leader of the action committee.
No arrests were made during the incident at the embassy.
Japanese deputy Shingo Nishimura, a conservative member of the opposition New Frontier Party, and three other people landed on one of islands on Tuesday and held a brief commemorative ceremony.
The act drew protests from China and Taiwan, which warned Japan against imprudent action that would jeopardise relations.
The Japanese-administered islands are claimed by Taiwan, Japan and China.
Taiwan's foreign minister John Chang summoned the unofficial Japanese envoy Toshio Goto on Wednesday to express the island's "indignant concern" over the landing.
Roy Wu, ministry spokesman, told reporters that Chang also gave the envoy a statement to be given to the Japanese government to express Taiwan's firm stance on sovereingty over the Diaoyu islands.
Ching Chia-shou later said his committee would join forces with activists from Hong Kong to declare "our sovereignty over the Diaoyu islands".
"We are planning a large-scale action on May 18, taking boats to near the Diaoyus and (will) swim ashore. We plan to land on the island and stay there overnight," he said.
But Roy Wu asked activists to remain rational.
"The government emphasises on peace and ration in settling the dispute," he said.
The cluster of uninhabited islands has ignited nationalist passions in China, Taiwan and Hong Kong since a Japanese right-wing group built a makeshift lighthouse there last July.
The lighthouse drew protest flotillas to the islands and a Hong Kong activist drowned last September when he jumped into stormy waters near the islands to press China's claim.
Waters surrounding the islands are rich fishing grounds and are believed to contain unexploited oil and gas reserves.
